review_text_clean: Absolutely obnoxious. I'm not averse to difficult games, but Devil's Dive is difficult in an annoying way, not an engaging way. Hitboxes are unreadable, environmental hazards are obscured by the viewport, character acceleration swings wildly upon input. The game does not respect your time whatsoever. DD also tries to be a more feature-rich version of Downwell but misses the point that simplicity is one of the things that makes Downwell great. For example, the 360-degree aiming doesn't really add anything to the gameplay, but it does necessitate more awkward controls on a gamepad. Why would a platformer use an aim design that requires migrating the jump command from a face button to a shoulder button? It is different, but it's not better - I'd say it's actually worse, since using a trigger to jump in any game has, and always will, feel awful. DD looks and sounds great, but, unless you enjoy a very specific kind of old-school, teeth-grinding difficulty, you will not find this game fun. Avoid.

No but seriously, the only thing I could think of while playing was that this is the kind of game the AVGN would get mad at. But unlike the nerd, I don't have to wonder what the developer was thinking; I know he intentionally designed the game to be frustrating, obscure and punishing. The game is clearly a sendup of old adventure games with light RPG elements, like a Sierra/Zelda 2 slurry. And man, it is wildly directionless and inscrutable. You're given almost no guidance, and after two hours of fumbling with the thing I'm still not sure where I was ever supposed to go. Combat is a frustrating mash fest that feels purely random whether you can kill an enemy without being hit in return. Healing is scarce and enemies respawn with each screen transition, so the game quickly becomes a dull slog running back to your bedroom to heal. Significant grinding seems almost mandatory with high item costs. The castle area is annoyingly large with few things to find, leading to most of your time being spent in transit. And God help you if you take a careless step: the princess will happily wander off an edge to her death. The front of the castle is surrounding by an instadeath moat that you must carefully path around or your big, triumphant return will become 20 mintues of lost progress in 1 second. It's a wildly frustrating and unsatisfying game, and the only reason I'm not leaving a red review is because this is a solo dev passion project and I can tell it was deliberately designed to be this way. For a masochist or someone seriously nostalgic for Sierra this is probably a great game. For anyone else, stay far away, especially at $20.

review_text_clean: Robogal is a blend of various puzzles and VN, and all sprinkled with hentai fanservice. An attractive mix (to me) at a budget price. Worth trying, or should you skip it? You play as an unnamed robot constructor, taking orders from clients. Your work requires you to build robot girls based on real women. In order to collect data, you need to locate and interact with target models. Seven women, to be precise. You find them on a city map, where you can click on their pictures. Clicking initiates a VN-style conversation, followed by a puzzle. Puzzles vary a bit. You could be swapping tiles to complete a picture, searching the black screen with a camera to locate your model, mixing colours in a specific order, etc. None of the puzzles pose a real challenge, and the majority can be done in less than 2–3 minutes. After several scenes, you can assemble the bio-robot and move on to another order. There is nothing innovative or creative, but at least there is some variety. Also, after assembling, you can 'test' your creation. Since this is a budget title, my expectations were low. Still, while the puzzles were ok, the English translation sucks. It is better than machine translation, but not by much. Also, the 'testing' option is rather bland. To be honest, for the price asked, the overall quality is acceptable. I was neither satisfied nor disappointed. Just mid. The character art was simply recycled from other games form this dev. I am familiar with most, if not all, of the characters you encounter. Maybe one or two character poses are new; that's it. Moreover, the 'testing' part, i.e., an interactive hentai scene, feels rather lacking. There are a very limited number of very short animation loops. While the quality is fine, I sure expected more. All are uncensored, at least. As for the backgrounds and the UI design, all are fairly good. Similarly to art, the music was also familiar to me. All tracks were present in the other games of this dev. Cost-cutting approach, but the track choices are ok. Nothing catchy or memorable, but they serve their role as background fillers well enough. For the asked price - acceptable. No bugs encountered. To conclude, this game is a low-cost mix of puzzles and badly translated stories. Art and music are fine, but the hentai part is lacking. For a budget price, you get budget entertainment. Only with low expectations is it possible to have fun playing: 4.7/10

review_text_clean: boring, bland, unintuitive The only good thing about this "game" is the awesome music, but that's only because Aweswan didn't make it themselves (the very first track is by TSFH). The camera control sucks. It scrolls suuuuper slow ... ... also, the map isn't a globe. That means the US is on the far left end and Japan on the far right end. If you wanna try to recreate WW2 and nuke Japan, you don't just cross the Pacific - you have to scroll aaaaall the way over there over the Atlantic, Europe, and Asia in slomo . I swear, the stupid plane carrying the Hiroshima bomb arrived faster in Japan than my mouse cursor did... Rest of the controls suck, too: The "game" has no shortcut keys, you have to do fu cking everything with the mouse. Graphics suck: The map is most probably from Google Images and there are no animations worth a damn. The attacks are "animated" with a few colored lines and the simplest of explosion gifs; but none of the catastrophes are animated... I mean, how cool (and easy to animate) would it have been to see an asteroid crash into the simplistic map? Speaking of the simplistic map: The game looks just plain boring. The sun's reflection in the ocean is the only good thing I remember about this lazy graphics. Wonder where Aweswan stole that from?... It's definitely not their own work. The "game" has a bajillion of cringeworthy typos. It would be somewhat forgivable, if the devs from Aweswan had another language than English, but since the devs apparently and fortunately no longer exist I couldn't find that out, so let's leave it with "learn to spell, you swanheads". Also, its mechanics make no sense. US and Russia start with no nukes? But the country I choose to start in has always 4 nukes, even if I start as Czechia, Congo, or Bhutan? And a few in-game years later literally everyone has nukes, even Tibetian monks!... Ridiculous. Imagine being afraid of nuking Liechtenstein or Andorra, because they might send some nukes back at you... -,- Also, while playing the game told me that Austria lost 120 million civilians. Last time I checked it had only about 9 million, though!?! And that RL number included civilians and military personell. Also, in my very first game Spain got immediately in turn 1 invaded and taken over by Andorra which evidently in the real world has no armed forces and is under Spain's protection... All that stupid stuff would've been okay, if it had been about some no-name fantasy countries in a fantasy world. Was it really that hard to come up with a fantasy world instead of this unrealistic immersion-breaking BS?...

review_text_clean: The best way to sum up KOTH is as a first-person, single-piece chess game. The movement is point-and-click, with some limitation. However you wish to classify it, it's a fun game. If you read other reviews or parts of the discussion boards, you'll run across the name "The Sentinel". KOTH is heavily influenced by this DOS game from 1986. Having never played The Sentinel myself, I'm coming into this experience with zero experience. The game is very easy to pick up, but has a slight learning curve. There are 2 modes: Classic and Arcade. In Arcade, you have no limit to moving around. If you can see a square, you can move to it. You will need to absorb trees in order to gain energy to build blocks, which are necessary to get to elevated parts of the topography. While in Classic, in order to move you will first need to place an "Avatar" for your character, then possess and snap to that space where you avatar once was. This is a much more challenging version of the game. You will need to absorb trees and place blocks just like in Arcade, but you'll need to be far more mindful of your energy use and re-absorption. As you may derive from the title, KOTH, is a game where you become King of the Hill. The cyclopic black tower in the center of every level is The KOTH. You must slay the creature by absorption and then replace it to win. This is why I think of it as a single-piece chess game as you move your character across a chess-board like environment with strategically raised plateau and layers. KOTH watches the outstretching board with a beam that destroys artificial structures you place, while leaving trees unharmed. If the beam touches you, you die. You'll respawn where you started, however, anything you collected along the way will be gone. I absolutely recommend checking out KOTH. If you're a casual player, completionist, speedrunner, or VR-enthusiast looking for an odd title to conquer, KOTH has something for you.

review_text_clean: This is a pretty good route for TS. It's not the best and it has its good and band points, but overall it's OK. The scenery and modelling is well done and is probably the best part of the addon. The West London Line is very well done and I use the line a lot in real life, and I have to say, it couldn't be much more accurate in this addon. The trains on the other hand, aren't so good. The class 375 is a good train, but the sounds are pretty bad. The door sounds are completely out of sync with the animations, not that this is uncommon for DTG addons... The sounds also take for ever to catch up when you go to a different view. Also, the cab is very generic and pretty much looks like it has been copied and pasted from all the other units that look similar from the outside. Some of the platforms are bugged, because when I stop the train sometimes, the doors in the first or last units do not open, even though I have stopped well within the middle of the platform. The class 170 is OK, but the sounds are not very accurate and acceleration tend to be slow. I have also found that they have chosen to include hardly any scenarios on the North London Line. All of them are on the GOBLIN. I think there is only one scenario which transversely the NLL. Personally for the expensive price, I would have liked to have seen some more scenarios for this part of the route. Why couldn't they have compiled some over from the old North London Line DLC? Anyway, overall I think the route is good, but the trains not so much. I feel that it may be a bit overpriced for what you get, and a lack of scenarios, so wait for a sale before buying it.

review_text_clean: Made it to the Championship three of my first four career seasons and was cheated out of the game all three times on the final play. WAY to much developer interference on every snap of every game. He seems to think his job was to find a way to cheat a human player on every play in some way, and all of his focus seems to have gone into that. He even goes so far as to claim the computer doesn't "know" what you enter for a play. Oh really? Then how does it run the play. The game is programmed to run when you call a pass defense, and pass when you call a run defense. On offense it runs out of pass formations routinely--especially when you call pass--and passes out of obvious run formations at least 50% of the time, unless you call a pass defense, of course Computer teams can run any running play out of an empty backfield, for instance, but a human player can run only a reverse. Computer teams can designate the HB hot receiver as primary receiver on long passes, but human coaches cannot. There are dozens of ways the developer figured out to screw you out of most anything you accomplish, and this seems to have been his main focus throughout the game. The game quite obviously runs on profiles, the developer made all of them, and a simple algorithm decides whether or not you win the game regardless of what you do as human coach. Might have been nice if the developer had actually watched a football game before he decided to design one. Alas, he clearly believes the point of the game is to manipulate the outcome artificially, primarily with turnovers and penalties but also with a huge array of artificial means wherever the developer's algorithm determines a timely monkey wrench is called for. The saddest thing about this game is how predictable it is. You can quite literally call most penalties and turnovers before they happen due to the developer's lack of imagination and his determination to manipulate the outcome of games.

review_text_clean: I can't recommend this game. Honestly, it's mid! It isn't terrible, but it's also not very good. As a long time BATIM fan, this is one of the most underwhelming sequels I've ever seen. the writing is mediocre, the sound design is erratic at times, and the random lag spikes make it incredibly frustrating to navigate around the cartoon world. The game mechanics themselves are downright infuriating, not to mention the false sense that there may be multiple endings scattered around the game. The mechanic where the ink demon shows up, and you're required to hide, is VERY underwhelming and has almost no sense of actual urgency other than forcing the player to drop everything and find the nearest barrel. The fact that combat stops you from hiding is also incredibly frustrating, and caused multiple unnecessary deaths when I would get ganged up on by lost ones during an inconvenient demon appearance. The visuals and music are, as usual, very good. The consistent designs and stylistic choices are pleasant on the eyes and never get too boring. It's a gorgeous game, I'll give it that! The ending is cheesy and undeserved, it didn't feel nearly as impactful as it was implied to be. The fact that the Big Steve quest can be entirely skipped makes his appearance useless, but the fact that everyone else shows up too just makes it feel like a fix-it fic rather than the ending to a saga. TL;DR - Overall, I give it a 4/10. It's painfully mediocre, and the gameplay far overshadows any meaningful worldbuilding or lore added throughout the entire experience. I recommend watching someone else play this, or just reading the wiki, rather than purchasing it and playing it for yourself. (SPOILERS FOR THE ENDING - but seeing the little baby bendy at the end of the game DID make me squeal with joy, so actually, 10/10 flawless game no notes)

This game is not ready for early access. I do not recommend it in its current state. I am not hopeful that this extremely basic game will grow into something worth playing, but I hope it does.

review_text_clean: I am halfway through the career scenarios and I must say I am really enjoying the route. The route is beautiful with a great mix of cities, small towns, and rural areas. There are several large yards for switching. There are 98 miles of mainline for long distance runs. There are passenger stations throughout the route, even on some of the branch lines. There are several unique assets, and most have winterization applied. There is a lot of rolling stock, including boxcars, hoppers, flatcars, tankers, and gondolas for hauling a variety of different freight. Many of these come in multiple liveries, including NYC, NH, PRR, and BA. There are passenger coaches and baggage cars in NYC and NH liveries. There are plenty of duties for each of the four locomotives that are provided with the route. According to many reviews, the RS3 is completely broken because it has a headlight issue where both the front and rear headlights are always on. While I have noticed this issue as well, it isn’t a major deal and will likely get fixed relatively soon. The locomotive appearances aren’t amazing but not bad either. These aren’t Searchlight Simulations quality, but they aren’t advertised as such either. For the most part, the physics and breaking systems run as I'd expect. I cannot comment on the sounds. I don’t know exactly what these locomotives should sound like. So that all being said - yes, I most definitely recommend this route.

You have a deck of cards that starts very simple, and every time you gain a level you can add new cards to your deck or upgrade your current ones. A genre that I mostly enjoy, the problems I have are the following: 1) The game does absolutely nothing new or exciting in any way, just the most basic forms of the genre 2) The UI is questionable at best, so you are often forced to guess at what potential upgrades might do 3) The resources you use to play cards accumulates so fast that you are just always playing all of your cards all the time, as fast as you can, which removes a lot of the strategy and also means: 4) you are trying to play your "cards" so fast that there is never any time to observe what is happening. review_text_clean: A very nice, very stylish, creative roguelite bullet-heaven game. The game isn't super long, took me about 6 hours to finish, would probably take about 30 more minutes for 100% of the achievements. The game has full controller support and nice accessibility options for modulating difficulty, not to mention the ability to pick your difficulty less directly within runs as well. The art is great (gives me Cowboy Bebop vibes, can't quite put my finger on why), the music is great, the story (surprised me that there was any!) is basic but touching, the gameplay is somewhat innovative (mixing Necrodancer-style rhythm-combat mechanics with Vampire Survivors-like top-down bullet-heaven combat) and is pretty fun, although it gets a little bit repetitive by the end. I hope there is a bit more exploration of unsteady rhythms if the devs ever make a next entry, there is a lot of leniency in getting 'perfect's here and after a while the consistent rhythm gets pretty second-nature, so it might be nice to see that shaken up. The game lacks polish, but not in any way that truly breaks the experience. It's mostly observed in some unintended behaviours¹, incorrect tooltips, etc. The main thing that diminishes the experience in my opinion is the lack of visual clarity on some levels and with some builds (looking at you, 'Chain projectiles'). I also think it would benefit from some more clarity on how its basic mechanics work (tagging weapons with their damage types, an option to show values in skill descriptions, etc.), the 15 tips on pause help but don't really explain everything (although with how short the experience is and with how not-that-difficult even the later stages are, you won't play for long enough for this lack of knowledge to sour your experience like it probably would in a 100+ hour game). Ah, also, for whatever reason, achievements aren't working at all for me (they don't even show up on the game's page in my library), although that might be Steam's fault.
